title: When The Executive Becomes The Crisis, Is Your Company Prepared?
summary: Crisis communications planning often focuses on what might happen to a company. NVIDIA is an important reminder to prepare just as seriously for crises that originate inside the organization.
body_markdown:
Companies often anticipate that a cyberattack, product failure, or natural disaster can trigger a crisis. But what happens when the crisis is sitting in the executive suite?


NVIDIA provides a striking example. CEO Jensen Huang recently acknowledged an affair with a business executive who may have been involved with the Chinese government. The company’s board subsequently launched an independent investigation, additional allegations of relationships between Huang and company employees were reported, and he has now resigned, with the company’s CFO taking over on an interim basis.


What started as a story about an executive’s personal conduct quickly expanded into questions about corporate governance, national security risk, impact on shareholder value, and the future of the company’s leadership. (NVIDIA has lost more than $500 billion in shareholder value since the news broke, and a lawsuit has already been filed alleging that the company and Huang misled investors.)


*This incident should make every communications leader ask: Are we prepared if one of our executives becomes the crisis?*


## **Why Executive Misconduct Presents A Unique Crisis Communications Challenge**


When executive misconduct occurs, this represents a particularly difficult crisis communications scenario, because the person normally expected to lead the organization through turmoil is instead its source. And when a high-profile CEO is closely associated with the corporate brand, such as the case with Huang, separating the reputation of the leader from that of the company becomes even harder.


Too many organizations remain[unprepared for crises](https://www.forrester.com/report/b2b-companies-lack-adequate-crisis-communications-preparedness/RES190757) of any kind. Forrester’s B2B Brand And Communications Survey from last year found that, even among larger companies, only 64% of marketing leaders said their organization updates crisis communications plans at least annually, and just 39% said it conducts annual crisis simulations or tabletop exercises.


NVIDIA demonstrates why simulations are critical and why they must go beyond familiar scenarios. An executive scandal is far-ranging and can trigger investigations, employee concerns, customer questions, investor scrutiny, litigation, government interest, and intense media attention almost simultaneously. Communications can’t manage those repercussions effectively when operating in react mode.


## **Prepare For The Crisis You Hope Never Happens**


What the NVIDIA imbroglio highlights is that companies should explicitly include executive misconduct in their[crisis communications planning](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/be-swift-be-accurate-be-empathetic-three-pillars-for-crisis-communications/) . This means proactively considering the possibilities; determining how the organization will operate when a senior leader’s judgment, credibility, or ability to lead comes into question publicly; and then testing those plans. Crisis communications leaders should coordinate the effort to:


- Determine who will take charge if the CEO can’t credibly serve as spokesperson.
- Establish communications decision rights among the board, communications leadership, legal, HR, security, investor relations, and other functions.
- Map the stakeholders who could be affected and the information that each will need.
- Determine what would trigger an independent investigation, leadership change, or additional disclosure.
- Prepare communications that explain not simply what happened but what the organization is doing to protect employees, customers, shareholders, and other stakeholders.


Crisis communications planning often focuses on what might *happen to* a company. NVIDIA is an important reminder to prepare just as seriously for crises that originate *inside* the organization. Rehearse scenarios involving executive misconduct, establish who will take control when a senior leader is compromised, and anticipate how the consequences could spread across the business. The time to determine how your organization will respond when a leader puts the company at risk is long before that leader actually does.
